title: Palm Sunday
hook: the palms and the long passion read with the whole congregation

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laetare, the rose halfway through Lent. Your line was halfway, rejoice. What did you celebrate in the middle of something long? Day six hundred fifty-eight.

Ushers stand at the door handing out strips of palm, and within a minute some kid is sword fighting with one, or folding it into a cross. The service begins outside, or at the back, with a procession and singing. Branches are waving. It feels like a parade. Then, not long after, the same congregation, holding the same palms, will be reading aloud a line nobody wants to say. This is a Sunday that turns around in the middle.
screen: `PALMS AT THE DOOR.` →`A PARADE WITH BRANCHES.` → `THE SUNDAY THAT TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the entry. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, a king's entrance done humbly, as the prophet Zechariah had pictured. People throw their cloaks and branches on the road and shout, in Matthew's account, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest." Hosanna is Hebrew, from Psalm 118: save, please. A cry for rescue that had become a shout of welcome. The palms are blessed and the people process, re-enacting it. Then the Mass begins, and the gospel is the Passion, the whole account of his arrest, trial and death, from Matthew, Mark or Luke depending on the year. It's long, and it may be read in parts. A reader narrates. The priest takes the words of Jesus. And the congregation reads the crowd. So the same voices that sang hosanna at the door find themselves saying, together, crucify him. That's deliberate. The Church isn't pointing at a crowd long ago and saying, look what they did. It's handing the line to everyone in the pews. Catholic teaching is clear that the blame for his death falls on all sinners, not on any one people. Hosanna, then crucify: the same mouths, the same week. People take the palms home and tuck them behind a crucifix or a picture, and next year, as Ash Wednesday's lesson told, palms like these become the ashes. And this week behind us: forty days, upon this rock, christ in every eye, the silent saint, be it done, halfway, rejoice. Now the week everything has pointed toward.
screen: `A KING ON A DONKEY.` · `HOSANNA: SAVE, PLEASE.` · `THE PASSION, IN PARTS.` · `THE PEOPLE READ THE CROWD.` · then, large: `HOSANNA, THEN CRUCIFY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a palm at home. If you have one from church, find a place for it: behind a crucifix, over a door, tucked into a picture frame. If you don't, find any green leaf or small branch and set it somewhere you'll see it this week. Sit with it. Think about how quickly cheering can turn, in a crowd, in a friendship, in yourself. If you pray, you can say the old cry, hosanna, save, please. If you don't, simply hold the leaf and the week ahead. The bell holds the time.
Palm Sunday. The Sunday before Easter: palms and a procession, then the Passion read aloud, with the congregation as the crowd. Today's word.
Your line: hosanna, then crucify. Today, notice when you're about to turn on someone you praised, and stop. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: On Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord, Catholics receive blessed palms, process into church, and hear the Passion read, sometimes in parts with the congregation reading the crowd; some keep the palms at home until next year's Ash Wednesday.

myth: it's Hebrew from Psalm 118: save, please.
Catholic teaching blames one people for Jesus's death
it teaches that the blame falls on all sinners, which is why the congregation reads the crowd.
in Matthew, the crowd spreads branches and cloaks on the road
and cries hosanna to the son of David.

fork.setup: you're in the pew, palm in hand. the Passion is being read in parts, and the crowd's line comes up. it's yours. what do you say?
options: skip it; it's not my line.
fork.reveal: the congregation reads the crowd: crucify him. the same voices that sang hosanna at the door. the Church hands the line to everyone.

original.note: Hebrew: save, please, from Psalm 118:25; the root of hosanna.

trapdoor: what you thought: Palm Sunday is a happy parade before Easter.
what it means: the day turns from hosanna at the door to crucify in the Passion, and the congregation says both.
what a scholar hears: hosanna is Hebrew hoshia na from Psalm 118:25; the entry echoes Zechariah 9:9; reading the Passion in parts places the guilt on all, not one people.

sources.quoted: Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest.

sources.ref: Catechism of the Catholic Church 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4

notes: Reading the Passion in parts with the congregation as the crowd is common practice but optional. Confirm 'in many parishes'.
Blame for the Passion: CCC 597–598 and Nostra Aetate 4 reject collective blame on the Jewish people and place responsibility on all sinners. Confirm phrasing.
Hebrew הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא in Psalm 118:25 (Hebrew numbering). Confirm pointing.
